results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
The IRS says you must keep your tax records “as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  In practice, that means:

* **Income‑tax records** are kept until the period of limitation for that return runs out (usually 3–6 years, depending on the situation) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* **Employment‑tax records** must be kept for at least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* **Asset‑related records** should be kept until the period of limitation expires for the year you dispose of the property [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
* If you no longer need records for tax purposes, do not discard them without checking whether other agencies (e.g., insurers, creditors) require a longer retention period [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several reasons that are spelled out in the IRS Publication 583:

* Record‑keeping helps you **monitor the progress of your business** and decide what changes to make.  
  “Good records will help you do the following. Monitor the progress of your business.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* They enable you to **prepare accurate financial statements**, such as income statements and balance sheets.  
  “Prepare your financial statements. You need good records to prepare accurate financial statements.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* They **support the items reported on your tax returns** so that the IRS can verify what you report without extra paperwork.  
  “Support items reported on tax returns. You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* They are required for compliance with the Internal Revenue Code, and must be kept for the period of the tax‑law limitation periods.  
  “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* Additionally, the publication states that keeping documents “supports the entries in your books and on your tax return.”  
  “It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
You decide on an accounting method when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business.  
· **Cash method** – You report income in the year you actually receive it and usually deduct expenses in the year you actually pay them.   
  - This is the simplest method and is used by many sole‑propietors who do **not have inventory**.   
  - If you do have inventory, the cash method is only allowed if your business qualifies as a *small‑business taxpayer* (see Pub. 538 for the definition).  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]  
· **Accrual method** – You report income when it is earned (even if payment comes later) and deduct or capitalize expenses when they are incurred, regardless of payment timing.  
  - This method is required when you keep inventory that is **necessary to account for your income** (unless you meet the small‑business exception above).  
  [cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)]  

If you later want to change methods, you normally must obtain IRS approval by filing Form 1128; a few special circumstances allow automatic approval.  
[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]  

**Summary** –  
• Use the cash method if you have no inventory, or if you are a small‑business taxpayer and your inventory can be treated as non‑incidental material or supplies.  
• Otherwise, use the accrual method.  
• Keep the same method for all income and for your books, and file Form 1128 to change.  
[cite this passage as: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)]

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To identify hazards in your workplace you should conduct routine *self‑inspections*:

1. **Perform a systematic walk‑through of the work area with knowledgeable employees** so they can spot potential hazards directly.  
2. **Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists** that cover general industry tasks (e.g., housekeeping, housekeeping, emergency routes, signage, recordkeeping) to ensure you evaluate common hazard areas.  
3. **Identify hazards, control them (engineering or administrative controls), and monitor the effectiveness of those controls during future inspections**.

These steps are described in the Small Business Safety and Health Handbook:

> “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i. e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly. Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to: • identify hazards, • control identified hazards, and • monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash‑method accounting records income and expenses in the year they are actually **received or paid**.  
Accrual‑method accounting records income in the year it is earned (when you have the right to receive it) and records expenses in the year they are **incurred** (when the liability is created), even if payment is made later.  

*From IRS Publication 334 (tax guide for small businesses):*

- “Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them …”  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)]

- “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.”  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)]

The purpose of the accrual method is to **match income and expenses in the correct year**.

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a business owner to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that are part of a trip away from home for business purposes.  This includes transportation, lodging, meals (subject to a 50 % limit), and other related costs such as telephone calls and tips.  

**Transportation and travel costs**

> “Transportation. You can deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and your business destination.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

> “Taxi, commuter bus, and limousine. You can deduct fares for these and other types of transportation between the airport or station and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location away from home.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

> “Car or truck. You can deduct the costs of operating and maintaining your vehicle when traveling away from home on business. You can deduct actual expenses or the standard mileage rate (discussed earlier under Car and Truck Expenses), as well as business‑related tolls and parking.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

> “If you rent a car while away from home on business, you can deduct only the business‑use portion of the expenses.”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

**Meals and other incidental items**

> “Meals and lodging. You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest to properly perform your duties. You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance to calculate your deduction. In most cases, you can deduct only 50% of your meal expenses.”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

> “Telephone. You can deduct the cost of business calls while on your business trip, including business communication by fax machine or other communication devices.”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

These passages show that business travel expenses are deductible when they are ordinary, necessary, and part of a trip away from home for business.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
**What the documents say about an executive summary**

The SBA Business Planning Guide explains that an executive summary is a **brief, one‑or‑two‑paragraph** section that gives the reader an overview of the business plan. It should include:

* a short description of the business idea  
* the amount of money needed and how it will be used  
* a brief schedule of key milestones or goals  

These points are taken directly from the guide’s “Business Plan Outline” section.  

> Executive Summary:  
> This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of what you want to accomplish. For example, describe your idea, how much money you need, what you need it for, how much money you will bring (or have put) into the business, and a brief schedule of your goals. Since you won’t know some of these facts until you complete your business plan, write this section last.  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market in a business plan, the **SBA Business Planning Guide** recommends the following steps:

1. **Identify the niche** – State who your “best” customers are.  
   - *“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Segment the market** – For business customers, use factors such as industry, company size, location, or product use/application.  
   - *“Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

   For consumer (household) markets, segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   - *“Consumer (household) markets might be segmented by demographics, (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate size and growth** – Use population figures, sales tax data, industry statistics, etc., to calculate the approximate size of the target market and its growth potential.  
   - *“Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Describe why your product/service fits** – Explain how your offering meets the needs or solves the problems of the identified customer group.  
   - *“Explain why customers will leave your competition and switch to your business. Also, describe what you will offer that your competitor can’t easily copy and what you will do to combat competitive reactions.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

5. **Quantify the market potential** – Include figures such as estimated customer numbers, buying frequency, and potential revenue contribution.  

By following these points—defining who the customers are, how you segment them, estimating the market size, and explaining the fit—you’ll create a clear, data‑supported target‑market description for your plan.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes. The ADA requires that any private business that serves the public—such as a shop—must remove physical barriers that are **“readily achievable.”**  
The guide explains:

> “If you own, operate, lease, or lease to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities as well as for compliance when a facility is altered or a new facility is constructed. … **You must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable,”** which means a barrier that can be removed with reasonable cost, time, or effort”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

Because your shop is a public‑accommodation, you must make it accessible if it can be done in a readily achievable way. This includes:

* Providing an accessible entrance (or a sign to an accessible entrance) – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
* Ensuring doors are at least 36 in wide and use accessible hardware (e.g., lever handles) – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
* Maintaining accessible aisles and counter heights that allow wheelchair use (e.g., a counter no higher than 38 in and a clear floor space of 30 in × 48 in in front of the counter) – [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
* Offering accessible parking and an accessible route from the parking to the entrance if possible – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).

If a barrier cannot be removed in a readily achievable manner, you must instead provide an alternative means of access or service (e.g., mobile assistance, home delivery). The ADA does not exempt existing facilities; they still must be brought into compliance to the extent they can be in a readily achievable way.

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
**To keep your employees safe**  
1. **Create and maintain a safety‑and‑health program**.  
   • State that such a program “prevents workplace injuries and illnesses, improves compliance with laws and regulations, and reduces costs” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6).  
   • The program must include: a written plan, frequent inspections, employee training, a system for reporting hazards, and continual evaluation of the program [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10).  
2. **Plan and maintain exits, exit paths, and emergency procedures**.  
   • Every exit door must be **side‑hinged, swing open, and free of locks or keys** when the building is occupied [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=23).  
   • All exit routes must be **unobstructed, clearly marked, and equipped with illuminated exit signs that read “EXIT” in lettering at least 6 in. high** [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=28).  
   • An **emergency action plan** must identify evacuation triggers, chain‑of‑command, evacuation routes, assembly points, and special assistance for people with disabilities [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26).  
3. **Use periodic workplace inspections** (self‑inspection checklists) to verify that all safety rules—machinery guarding, housekeeping, fire protection, etc.—are met (osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 8‑9).  

**To keep your premises accessible**  
1. **Accessible entrances**  
   • If a building has an inaccessible entry, you must **provide an accessible alternative entrance or add a ramp/handrail** that meets the ADA slope limits (maximum 1:12 for a new ramp, 1:20 for existing ramps with a 6‑in. rise) [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
   • The accessible entrance must be **open during all business hours** and the building must carry a sign directing customers to it [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  

2. **Accessible parking**  
   • For every **≤ 25 parking spaces** you must provide **1 accessible space**; for ≤ 50 spaces, **2;** for > 50 spaces, the number increases by 1 for every additional 50 spaces [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
   • An accessible space must have an **access aisle at least 5 ft. wide (car spaces) or 8 ft. wide (van spaces)** and a **clear vertical clearance of ≥ 98 in.** (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 8‑9).  
   • The space must be **on level ground** and **connected by an accessible route that has no steps or steep slopes** [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9).  

3. **Other accessibility features**  
   • All doors that serve as public entrances must be **fully operable with no keys or special knowledge**; if a door can only be opened from the inside, an alternative accessible entrance must be provided [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
   • Where a turnstile or security gate blocks a public entrance, you must **replace it with an accessible gate or create an alternate entrance** [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  

**Bottom line:**  
- **Implement a documented safety‑and‑health program** that includes inspections and training.  
- **Ensure all exits and emergency plans** meet OSHA’s exit‑route and emergency‑action‑plan requirements.  
- **Remove or modify architectural barriers** (ramps, doors, turnstiles) according to the ADA **“readily achievable”** standard and provide accessible parking and routes as the ADA Manual requires.  

These steps come directly from the OSHA Small Business Safety & Health Handbook and the ADA Guide for Small Businesses.

The publication explains: “An accounting method is a set of rules used to determine when and how income and expenses are reported. You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return. runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
Business records are required for several practical and legal reasons:

* They **support the entries in your books and on your tax return**.  
  The IRS requires that you keep records that substantiate all income, expenses and credits you report.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

* They help you **monitor the progress of your business** and prepare accurate financial statements (income statements and balance sheets).  
  Good records let you see whether your business is improving, which items are selling, and what changes you need to make.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

* They facilitate **banking and credit activities**.  
  Records such as receipts, invoices and bank statements help when dealing with banks or creditors.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

* They ensure **compliance with federal tax deadlines and limitations**.  
  You must keep records for as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code, typically until the period of limitations for the related tax return expires.  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* They allow you to **respond to IRS or other inspections** quickly and accurately because a complete set of records speeds up examinations.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS gives you two primary accounting methods to choose from when you file your first business tax return, and it tells you when each method is required.

**1. Cash method**  
*Under the cash method you report income in the year you actually receive it, and you usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them.*  
[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]

Small‑business owners who **do not keep inventory** find the cash method the easiest to maintain. The IRS says that most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use it because it is simpler.  
[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]

**2. Accrual method**  
*Under the accrual method you generally report income in the year you earn it, even if payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them.*  
[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]

If your business **requires inventory** (goods held for sale, raw materials, or supplies that become part of a product), the IRS requires the accrual method, unless you are a “small business taxpayer” and choose a special inventory treatment that treats inventory as non‑incidental or conforms to your financial accounting.  
[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)]  
[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)]

**3. Other possibilities**  

- **Combination method** – you can combine cash and accrual elements for different items, but the rules are strict (e.g., if inventory is involved you must use accrual for purchases and sales).  
[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)]  
- **Special methods** – special rules apply to certain items of income or expense; you may need to seek IRS approval to change methods after the first return.  
[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]

**Choosing the method**

| Situation | Recommended method | Why |
|-----------|--------------------|-----|
| No inventory, simple bookkeeping | Cash | Simpler, IRS encourages cash for small businesses without inventory. |
| Inventory required | Accrual (or special inventory rule if small‑business) | Accrual matches income and expenses and satisfies the inventory requirement. |
| You want to combine methods | Combination, but follow the strict rules on inventory, matching, and consistency. | Allows flexibility but can be complex. |

**Steps to decide**  
1. **Determine if you maintain inventory.**  
   *If yes, lean toward accrual unless you qualify for the small‑business inventory exception.*  
2. **Consider bookkeeping resources.**  
   *Cash is easier to set up with simple checkbooks or single-entry records; accrual typically needs double‑entry or computerized software.*  
3. **File your first Schedule C (Form 1040) using the chosen method.**  
   *If you change later, you must generally get IRS approval with Form 1128.*  

In short, if your business has no inventory and you prefer a straightforward system, use the cash method; if you sell or produce goods that you keep in stock, use the accrual method (or the small‑business inventory special rule). Use the citations above for the precise IRS guidance.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To identify hazards in your workplace, use the OSHA Small Business Safety & Health Handbook’s routine self‑inspection approach. The handbook explains that:

* An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

* Small‑business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to:  
  – identify hazards,  
  – control identified hazards, and  
  – monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

* The handbook provides self‑inspection checklists that serve as a starting point for identifying hazards. These checklists can help you see where to begin taking action to make your business safer and more healthful for workers.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

* After completing a checklist, compile the information with injury and illness records, worker training data, and process/equipment information. This combined data helps determine where challenges exist and what controls are needed.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

* OSHA also offers on‑site consultation programs and other resources to help small‑business employers with the self‑inspection process at no cost.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

Thus, the recommended procedure is to schedule regular self‑inspections, use the handbook’s checklists to guide the review, record findings in a standardized form, and then use that data to plan and verify effective hazard controls.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes. Ordinary and necessary expenses incurred while traveling away from home for business are deductible. The deduction includes transportation, lodging, meals (50 % of the cost when you use actual expenses), telephone, tips, and other travel‑related costs.  

The rules are found in the IRS Small Business Tax Guide:

- “Travel expenses. These are the ordinary and necessary expenses of traveling away from home for your business … You can deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and your business destination.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

- “Meals and lodging. You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight … You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance to calculate your deduction. In most cases, you can deduct only 50 % of your meal expenses.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

- “Telephone. You can deduct the cost of business calls while on your business trip, including business communication by fax machine or other communication devices.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

To qualify, the trip must be **away from home** (defined as your tax home) for longer than a normal day and require sleep or rest to perform your duties. You may only deduct the portion of transportation costs that is for business use. The above passages outline the exact types of expenses that are deductible.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  
Because your shop serves the public, it is considered a **public accommodation** under the ADA, and you are required to remove “physical barriers” that are **readily achievable**【ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 6】.  
That obligation applies to existing facilities as well as to any alterations or new construction, and it is not waived by a grandfather provision except that the standards for buildings built before 1993 are less stringent【ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 6】.  

For a shop, the most common required changes are:

1. **Accessible entrance** – If the shop has two entrances, at least one must be accessible. You must make an entrance available that can be reached without steps or steep slopes, and it must be wider than 36 inches (or 32 inches for an older door that can be widened)【ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 10】.  
2. **Accessible sales or service counter** – The counter should be at least 36 inches long and no more than 36 inches high, with a cleared space of at least 30 × 48 inches in front so a wheelchair can pull alongside【ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 15】.  
3. **Accessible path of travel** – From the entrance to any area where goods or services are provided, the path must be at least 36 inches wide (or wider at turns) and have no steps or dangerous slopes【ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 10】.  

If these improvements are not **readily achievable** (i.e., they would cost more than a few hundred dollars, require major structural changes, or require the building to be taken out of service for an impractical amount of time), you can seek a waiver or demonstrate that the barrier removal would be imprudent. However, the default position is that you must take reasonable steps to make the shop accessible to people who use wheelchairs.

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Tax‑related records**

| Type of record | What to keep | Retention period (IRS rule) |
|----------------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| **General business records** (income, expenses, payroll, etc.) | All documents supporting the items reported on a tax return – sales slips, invoices, bank statements, canceled checks, employee time and payroll records, etc. | Keep **as long as records may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**; that means *supporting an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out*【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16】. |
| **Employment‑tax records** (e.g., Forms 941, W‑2, W‑3, 1099) | All documents on which the employment‑tax amounts are based, and the tax returns filed. | **At least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16】. |
| **Asset‑related records** (purchase, depreciation, sale, disposal) | Purchase invoices, title or bill of sale, depreciation schedules, sale agreements, etc. | Keep **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the asset is disposed of**【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16】. |
| **Filed tax returns** | Copies of the return itself (for reference and audit purposes). | Keep **for the same period as the supporting records** – typically the same as the period of limitations for the return【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16】. |

---

**Injury‑and‑illness records (OSHA)**

| Item | What to keep | Retention period (OSHA rule) |
|------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| **OSHA Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | A record of every occupational injury or illness that is recordable. | **At least 5 years** at the worksite【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |
| **OSHA Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) | A supplemental record of each recordable injury or illness. | Same 5‑year period as Form 300【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |
| **OSHA Form 300A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) | Annual summary of the Form 300 and 301 data. | At least **5 years** at the worksite【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |
| **Fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or loss‑of‑eye reports** | Any report required by OSHA that must be made to OSHA (e.g., within 8 hours for a fatality, within 24 hours for hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye). | These reports must be made **within the specified time frame** and the related information must be kept for at least 5 years【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |
| **Worker medical and exposure records** | Medical records and exposure data related to occupational illness or injury. | Retained for the **time period required for each specific type of record**【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |
| **Worker training records** | Documentation showing that training on safety and health hazards was provided. | Kept **as required by OSHA standards**; generally for the period covered by OSHA training retention guidelines【osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15】. |

---

**Summary**

- For **tax purposes**, keep all financial and supporting documents for as long as the IRS may need them to administer the tax law—generally the period of limitations (3–6 years, depending on the return) for income or deduction claims, 4 years for employment taxes, and until the end of the period of limitations for asset disposals.  
- For **injury and illness records**, retain OSHA forms 300, 301, and 300A, plus any fatality or severe‑injury reports, for **at least 5 years** at the worksite, and keep worker medical, exposure, and training records for the period required by OSHA or the specific record type.  

These retention schedules are pulled directly from the IRS Publication 583 (page 16) and the OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook (page 15).

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
Here’s a step‑by‑step path you can follow that the company’s own documents recommend for starting a business and keeping its taxes organized:

1. **Choose a business structure**  
   • Decide whether you’ll operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, or corporation.  
   • The SBA guide explains the key distinctions and what forms you’ll need: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

2. **Register your business name and obtain an EIN**  
   • File a fictitious‑name statement if you’re a sole proprietorship or partnership whose name does not include the owners’ last names.  
   • Any business that hires employees, has an employer‑identification number (EIN), or pays excise tax must get an EIN.  
   • The SBA guide lists the Secretary‑of‑State office (SDSOS.gov) or county Register of Deeds as contacts for filing. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
   • The IRS Publication 583 explains how to apply for an EIN (online, by mail, fax, or phone) and the timing you should aim for: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

3. **Select an accounting method**  
   • You can use the cash method (record revenue when received, expenses when paid) or the accrual method (record when earned or earned).  
   • Choose the method that best shows your income; you may need IRS approval if you switch later. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

4. **Set up a record‑keeping system**  
   • Keep receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll records, and any photos of business‑related expenses.  
   • A structured system lets you monitor progress, prepare financial statements, and provide documentation for tax returns. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

5. **Track and deduct business expenses**  
   • Ordinary and necessary expenses are deductible. Typical start‑up costs may be deducted up to $5,000 (or amortized if they exceed $50,000). [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=9)  
   • Record every expense as soon as it occurs to avoid missing deductions.

6. **File the correct tax returns**  
   • Depending on your structure, you’ll file an annual income‑tax return (e.g., Form 1040‑C for a corporation, Form 1040‑Schedule C for a sole proprietor).  
   • If you have employees, file the appropriate payroll taxes (Form 941, 944, etc.) and keep copies of required employee paperwork (W‑4, I‑9).  
   • Use the IRS Interactive Tax Assistant (IRS.gov/Help/ITA) or the guidance in Publication 583 to determine due dates and forms. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=24)

7. **Use available resources**  
   • The SBA website, local Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), and SCORE offer free counseling and templates to help you set up your business plan and keep records organized. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   • IRS tools like the online EIN application, withholding estimator, and tax‑help pages provide additional support. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=24)

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
**How to keep your employees safe**

1. **Perform routine self‑inspections** – a knowledge‑based check of every work area to identify hazards, control them, and evaluate that the controls remain effective.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

2. **Keep walking‑working surfaces clear, dry and in good repair** – holes, nails, spills, wet surfaces and obstructions must be fixed or removed immediately.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)  

3. **Provide adequate head‑room, guardrails and fall protection** whenever walking surfaces are elevated more than 4 ft (1.2 m).  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)  

4. **Maintain a clean, orderly, and sanitary work environment** – clear space around equipment, and maintain seating, restrooms, and sanitation.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Post required safety information** – a free OSHA job‑safety and health poster, the annual Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses (Form 300A) and any OSHA citations until the violation is corrected.  
   [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=13)  

6. **Use the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program** – a free, confidential program that helps small businesses spot hazards and develop solutions.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  

**How to keep your premises accessible for people with disabilities**

1. **Make sure at least one entrance is physically accessible** – provide a ramp, handrails, or a wide enough opening (at least 32 inches) and ensure any alternative entrance is open during business hours.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

2. **Install and tape a sign that points to accessible entrances** whenever a main entrance is not accessible.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

3. **Provide accessible parking spaces** – a space wide enough for a vehicle, an access aisle at least 8 ft wide (or 10 ft for vans), clear signage with the International Symbol of Accessibility, and an accessible route to the entrance.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  

4. **Maintain an accessible route** that has no steps or steep slopes, a firm, slip‑resistant surface, and a vertical clearance of at least 98 in.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  

5. **If a turnstile or other barrier is present**, remove it or replace it with an accessible gate, or provide an alternative entrance that can be used by someone with a wheelchair, walker, or cane.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)  

By following the self‑inspection checklist, keeping walkways and fall‑protection systems in good condition, posting required safety signs, and ensuring at least one entrance, accessible parking, and an accessible route are available and maintained, you can protect both the safety of your employees and the accessibility of your premises.

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Start with the outline** – the SBA Handbook gives a ready‑made skeleton for every plan.  
   *Executive Summary, Business, Management, Market, Money, Exhibits* are the six core sections.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*

2. **Fill in each section**  
   * **Business** – describe the product/service, industry, competitors, regulatory environment, licenses, facilities and equipment.  
     *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)*  
   * **Management** – name owners, ownership percentages, key staff and their duties, and note who will handle accounting.  
     *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)*  
   * **Market** – define the target market, estimate size, analyze competition, and outline your pricing, promotion, and distribution plan.  
     *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)* * *[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)*  
   * **Money** – prepare financial projections (3‑year income, cash flow, balance sheet) and a break‑even analysis.  Include a Sources‑and‑Uses of Funds sheet and a summary of financial need.  
     *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)*  
   * **Exhibits** – attach resumes, lease agreements, contracts, credit reports, and any other supporting docs.  
     *[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=17)*  

3. **Use the SBA’s ready‑made checklists and worksheets** for each section. The handbook warns you to “write the Executive Summary last” because it pulls together information you’ve gathered elsewhere.  
   *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)*

---

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Choose a tax year**  
   *Calendar year* if you have no books or a short fiscal period; otherwise you can select a *fiscal year*.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)*

2. **Select an accounting method**  
   *Cash method* – record income when received and expenses when paid.  
   *Accrual method* – record income when earned and expenses when incurred, even if not yet paid.  
   Pick one consistent with how you’ll report income and keep your books.  
   *[[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)*

3. **Decide on a bookkeeping system**  
   *Single‑entry* is simplest but may not suit larger or inventory‑heavy businesses.  
   *Double‑entry* gives built‑in checks and balances and is generally safer for most small businesses.  
   *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*

4. **Open a dedicated business checking account** and keep it separate from personal funds.  
   The handbook calls this the “business checkbook” and recommends depositing daily receipts there.  
   *[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

5. **Record transactions promptly** – use a daily summary of cash receipts and a monthly summary of cash receipts and disbursements.  
   *[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

6. **Reconcile regularly** – at least once a month, match your bank statement with your checkbook and journals to catch errors early.  
   *[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)*

7. **Maintain proper documentation** – keep invoices, receipts, canceled checks, bank statements, and detailed account descriptions.  
   *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*

8. **Use software if needed** – many small‑business packages exist. If you do, keep a clear journal, ledger, and chart of accounts, and produce machine‑readable copies that match the paper records.  
   *[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)*

---

**Putting It All Together**

* Finish the plan – use the SBA outline, complete the financial sheets, and attach exhibits.  
* Set up your chart of accounts, choose the tax year and accounting method, and open your business bank account.  
* Begin recording every transaction immediately and reconcile each month to keep the books accurate and ready for any lender or tax audit.

These steps come straight from the documents in this workspace. If you need specific line‑by‑line examples or templates, the SBA guide provides worksheets on the back pages; the IRS publication supplies the legal and recordkeeping rules.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
Yes. The IRS requires you to have a taxpayer identification number (TIN) so that it can process your business returns. For most small‑business owners that TIN is an **Employer Identification Number (EIN)**.  
- The IRS states that “You must have a TIN so the IRS can process your returns.” and that the EIN “is issued to individuals (sole proprietors), partnerships, corporations, and other entities by the IRS” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).  
- The Publication 334 notes that an EIN is also required “if you pay wages to one or more employees or file pension or excise tax returns” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  

When you file your first income‑tax return you must also **select an accounting method**. The IRS offers two basic methods:  

1. **Cash method** – report income when received and expenses when paid.  
2. **Accrual method** – report income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of payment date.  

The publication says, “You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return. There are two basic accounting methods” and then lists the cash and accrual methods [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

So, you need an EIN if you are required to file employee or certain tax returns, and you must pick either the cash or accrual accounting method at the time you file your first return.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
Keep your tax‑related records for the period of time that the IRS requires—generally the length of the period of limitations for each item.  As the publication states, you must retain records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until that item’s period of limitations expires.  Typical limits are:

* **Income‑tax returns** – 3 years unless you omitted large amounts of income (then 6 years) or filed a fraudulent return (no limit).  
* **Employment taxes** – at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS articles that set out the rules for choosing an accounting method are Pub. 583 *Beginning a Business* and Pub. 334 *Tax Guide for Small Businesses*.  They explain that you must pick a method when you file your first income‑tax return that includes the business schedule (e.g., Schedule C for a sole‑proprietor or partnership).

**What accounting methods are available?**  
In Pub. 583, 5 shows that the two basic methods are:

* **Cash method** – you record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  
* **Accrual method** – you record income when you earn it (even if payment is received later) and expenses when you incur them (even if payment is made later).  

(cite: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5))

**When each method is required**

* **Cash method** is allowed for most sole‑proprietors or partners *unless* the business keeps inventory.  If inventory is necessary, you must normally use the accrual method (or a special inventory method) (cite: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)).  
* Pub. 334, page 15, confirms that if your business has inventory you must use an accrual method for purchases and sales, except for very small businesses that qualify as “small‑business taxpayers” and can treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies.  (“If an inventory is necessary … you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for your sales and purchases.”) (cite: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15))  
* Pub. 334, page 16, notes that a small‑business taxpayer that does **not** keep inventory can still choose the cash method and treat inventory items as non‑incidental material or supplies, thereby avoiding the accrual requirement. (cite: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16))

**How to decide**

1. **Does your business keep inventory?**  
   * *Yes*: you must use the accrual method for inventory sales and purchases.  If you are a very small business, you can still choose cash for other items, but inventory must be accrued.  
   * *No*: you may use the cash method—this is simpler because you only record money that actually moves in and out of the business.

2. **How large is your business?**  
   * If you are a very small business (see the definition of “small‑business taxpayer” in the IRS guidance), you may be able to keep inventory without adopting accrual accounting, but you must still use an accounting method that *clearly shows your income* (cite: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)).

3. **Plan for the future**  
   * If you anticipate adding inventory later, it is easier to start with accrual now and avoid a later change of method.  A change in accounting method usually requires IRS approval via Form 1128 (see Pub. 334, page 15).  

**Summary**

- **Use the cash method** if you *do not keep inventory* and want the simplest bookkeeping.  
- **Use the accrual method** if you *do keep inventory* (unless you qualify as a very small business that can treat inventory as non‑incidental supplies).  
- If you’re unsure whether your business qualifies as a small‑business taxpayer or whether it truly needs inventory, it is safest to start with the cash method and seek IRS guidance before adding inventory.  (cite: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16))

These are the only regulations that describe which accounting method you should use, and they are found explicitly in the IRS publications above.

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the procedure outlined in OSHA’s Small Business Safety and Health Handbook:

1. **Conduct routine workplace self‑inspections.**  
   “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklists to guide the inspection.**  
   “The checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces, but not for construction or maritime industries. They are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

3. **Document what you find.**  
   The handbook provides a template:  
   * Company name, worksite, specific worksite area, inspected by, date, and a simple “Yes/No/ N/A” format for key safety areas.  
   * Record any hazards found, how you control them, and whether the controls remain effective.

4. **Compile and cross‑reference data.**  
   “Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information (e.g., maintenance logs, failure incident reports) to help you determine where challenges exist.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

5. **Consult additional resources if needed.**  
   A small‑business employer may also request help from OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program, which offers free, confidential assistance with hazard identification and control. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

By following this process—routine self‑inspection, using the handbook’s checklists, recording findings, and integrating related records—you will be able to systematically identify, control, and monitor hazards in your workplace.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash and accrual accounting differ in **when income and expenses are reported**.

**Cash method**  
- You report income only when you actually receive it (or are constructively received) in the tax year.  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.  
- A business can use this method if it has no inventory or is a small‑business taxpayer that can treat inventories as non‑incidental supplies.  
  — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Accrual method**  
- You report income in the tax year the income is earned, even if the payment is received later.  
- You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year the expense is incurred, whether or not you pay it that year.  
- This method is required if you have inventory, because inventory must be accounted for in the year it is purchased and sold.  
  — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes. The IRS allows you to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that you incur while traveling for business **if the trip takes you away from home** (your “tax home”) for a period that is longer than an ordinary day’s work and you need to sleep or rest in order to perform your duties. The deduction can include:

* **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, taxi, limousine, or car rental between your home and the business destination, and between the airport/rail station and your hotel or work location.
* **Meals and lodging** – you may deduct the cost of meals and lodging provided the trip is overnight or long‑enough that you need a rest stop.  You may take the actual amount or use the standard meal allowance (generally 50 % of the cost).  
* **Vehicle expenses** – if you use your own vehicle for the trip, you may deduct either your actual expenses or the standard mileage rate (plus business‑related tolls and parking).  
* **Other related costs** – baggage and shipping, business telephone calls, and other expenses that are directly tied to the trip.

These rules apply to expenses required for travel on an **ordinary and necessary** basis (IRS § 170).  The following excerpt from *Publication 334 – Tax Guide for Small Businesses* explains the criteria and the types of travel expenses you can deduct:

> “Travel expenses. These are the ordinary and necessary expenses of traveling away from home for your business. You are traveling away from home if both the following conditions are met.  
>  1. Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work.  
>  2. You need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away from home.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

It then details the deductible categories:

> “You can deduct the cost of transportation … between your home and your business destination.  
>  You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest to properly perform your duties… You can deduct the cost of business calls while on your business trip, including business communication by fax machine or other communication devices.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

Therefore, if your travel qualifies under the “away‑from‑home” definition, you can deduct the relevant costs listed above.  Be sure to keep records that show the business purpose, dates, and expenses, as required by the IRS for substantiation.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
Yes—OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping rules give a partial exemption for certain small or low‑hazard employers.

* The Handbook says:

(osh​a_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 14)

“**All work‑related fatalities are reported to OSHA within 8 hours. All work‑related inpatient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye are reported to OSHA within 24 hours.**”  
(osh​a_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15)

So if you had 10 or fewer workers all last year, or you work in a designated low‑hazard industry, you are exempt from keeping OSHA Forms 300 and 301, but you must still meet the reporting deadlines above.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You need an **Employer Identification Number (EIN)** when:

* you **pay wages to one or more employees**;  
* you **file pension or excise tax returns**;  
* you operate as a **partnership, corporation, LLC, or other business entity** (the EIN is issued to these entities and to sole proprietors who choose to use one).  

These rules are stated in the IRS Small‑Business Guide:  

> “You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do … Pay wages to one or more employees … File pension or excise tax returns.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

> “EINs are assigned to sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and other entities by the IRS.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  

The **accounting method** is not tied to the EIN. When you file your first income‑tax return you choose an accounting method (cash or accrual). The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN. The IRS explains the two basic methods as:

> “You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return. There are two basic accounting methods. 1. Cash method ... 2. Accrual method …” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

If your business has inventory you are generally required to use the accrual method; otherwise many small businesses elect the cash method. The accounting method must remain the same for each tax year unless you get IRS approval to change it.

runs.question: how do i register a trademark
runs.answer:
To register a trademark for your business you can do it either at the **state** level or at the **federal** level.

1. **Choose the level of registration** – a state registration is handled by that state’s Secretary of State office, while a federal registration is handled by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).

2. **Search existing trademarks** – before filing you should search the trademark databases to make sure no one else has already registered the name you want.

3. **File the application**  
   * **State registration** – file with the Secretary of State.  In South Dakota, you can contact the Secretary of State at (605) 773‑2797 or visit https://sdsos.gov/.  
   * **Federal registration** – file with the USPTO.  Contact the USPTO at (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or visit www.uspto.gov.  

Doing this gives you the exclusive right to use the trademark or service mark for your business.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
For a new business the IRS tells you that you must pick one of two basic accounting methods when you file your first income‑tax return: the **cash method** or the **accrual method**.  
*Cash method*: you report income in the year you receive it and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them.  
*Accrual method*: you report income in the year you earn it—even if you receive payment later—and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

Whether you can use the cash method depends on whether inventory is required for your business:

- If your business **does not have inventory**, the cash method is generally appropriate.  
- If your business **needs inventory**, you must **use the accrual method** for purchases and sales.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

However, the IRS allows an exemption for small‑business taxpayers: a small‑business taxpayer can use the **cash method even if they have some inventory**, provided they treat those items as materials and supplies that are *not* incidental.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

So, choose the cash method if you have no inventory or if you are a small‑business taxpayer able to treat inventory as non‑incidental materials; otherwise, use the accrual method.

1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

runs.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
runs.answer:
Small‑business owners can identify and control workplace hazards by performing routine **self‑inspections**.  
The OSHA Small‑Business Safety and Health Handbook says:

*“An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.”*  
(osh\_small\_business\_handbook.pdf, page 8)

The handbook recommends that each inspection:

* identify hazards,
* control any hazards found,
* monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of those controls over time.  
(osh\_small\_business\_handbook.pdf, page 8)

To make inspections systematic, the handbook supplies **self‑inspection checklists** that cover general industry workplaces (not construction or maritime).  A checklist begins with pieces of basic work‑site information and then lists key hazard categories (safety‑and‑health programs, housekeeping, emergency routes, etc.).  
(osh\_small\_business\_handbook.pdf, page 8)

After completing a checklist you should:
1. collect the results,
2. combine them with injury/illness records, training logs, and equipment maintenance records,
3. use that combined data to determine where the biggest hazards or control gaps exist,
4. look up solutions in OSHA standards or other resources linked at the end of each checklist.  
(osh\_small\_business\_handbook.pdf, page 8)

*An example of a checklist format is shown on page 9, which records the name of the company, work area, inspector, date, and then a series of yes/no questions for each hazard category.*  
(osh\_small\_business\_handbook.pdf, page 9)

By conducting these routine self‑inspections, you create a systematic way to spot hazards, assess their control, and verify that your safety and health program remains effective.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a deduction for ordinary and necessary travel expenses incurred while you are away from home for business.  The requirements are:

* “travel… away from home” means the trip must be long enough that **you need to get sleep or rest to perform your duties** and it must take you **away from the general area of your tax home** (with your home being your regular place of business). – [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

* You may deduct the cost of **transportation** (air, train, bus, car, taxi, limousine, etc.) between your home and the business destination.  
* You may deduct the cost of **lodging** and **catering** for meals while the trip is overnight or long enough for sleep.  (In most cases, only **50 % of meal expenses** are deductible.) – [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

Thus, if your trip meets the “away‑from‑home” test, you can claim transportation, lodging, and (partial) meal expenses as deductions on your Schedule C (Form 1040).

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Starting a business and keeping your taxes organized**

1. **Decide what kind of business you’ll run**  
   * The most common forms are **sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation**—and you must choose the right one before you put a name on a tax return or apply for a business license.  
   * “The most common forms of business are the **sole proprietorship, partnership, and corporation**. When beginning a business, you must decide which form of business to use.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
   * “Do I have to start my tax year in January, or may I start it in any other month? See Designating a Tax Year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN)**  
   * All businesses that have employees, or that choose a corporation or partnership, need an EIN.  
   * “If your business will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer's Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained from Internal Revenue Service.”   
   * “Sole proprietors without employees may also choose to obtain a Tax ID number to use in place of their social security number for the business ID number.” 

3. **Write a business plan** (helps you stay organized and is often required by lenders)  
   * The handbook recommends a basic outline that includes an executive summary, market analysis, management structure, and financial “Money” section.  
   * “Developing a business plan is the first step to a successful business” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   * “The Money section of your business plan will show past, current and projected financial activity. Documents that should be included in your business plan... 3‑Year Income Projection, Statement of Cash Flow, Balance Sheet, and Break‑Even Analysis.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)

4. **Set up a bookkeeping system**  
   * Choose **single‑entry** (simple and uses cash receipts) or **double‑entry** (more accurate and gives built‑in checks).  
   * “…you may find the double‑entry system better because it has built‑in checks and balances to assure accuracy and control.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
   * “A good record‑keeping system includes a summary of your business transactions…in books (e.g., accounting journals and ledgers).” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   * When you start, keep a **daily summary of cash receipts** and **monthly summaries** to support the income statement.  
   * “The example illustrates a single‑entry system…Henry Brown, who is the sole proprietor of a small automobile body shop…” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

5. **Gather and keep supporting documents**  
   * Receipts, invoices, cancelled checks, payroll records, and receipts for business‑use home expenses must be retained to substantiate deductions.  
   * “These documents... support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  
   * “Keep them in an orderly fashion and in a safe place. For instance, organize them by year and type of income or expense.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

6. **Know how long to keep records**  
   * For most tax‑related records, keep them **until the period of limitations for that return runs out**.  
   * “How long must I keep them?…You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   * “Keep them for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later, if you have employees.” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

7. **Prepare and file your tax returns on time**  
   * Use your bookkeeping records to fill out the appropriate Schedule (e.g., Schedule C for sole proprietors).  
   * “You must keep supporting documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

By following the steps above—choosing the correct business structure, obtaining an EIN, crafting a thorough business plan, establishing a bookkeeping system, keeping all receipts and records in order, and retaining them for the required periods—you’ll set a solid foundation for your business and keep your federal tax responsibilities under control.
